title: Imam al-Ash'ari
hook: a star pupil of the Mu'tazilah changes his mind, and keeps his tools

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trial of the created Qur'an, and your line: the state stepped in. Ahmad ibn Hanbal held his ground in prison. Today, a scholar who left his first school. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

Three brothers. One grows up and dies a faithful believer. One grows up and dies rejecting faith. The third dies as a small child. Where does each one stand on the Day of Judgment? That puzzle, the later sources say, was put by a student in Basra to his teacher, al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazili master. The student was Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari. He had studied Mu'tazili theology for years and could argue it with skill. And by the time the conversation was over, the story goes, he had started to leave it. Today, a man who changed his mind, and kept his tools.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS.` → `A STUDENT'S PUZZLE.` → `A MIND STARTS TO CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of the story as it's told. The teacher answers: the believer in a high rank, the unbeliever punished, the child somewhere safe but lower, since he did no good works. The student presses: what if the child says, Lord, why didn't You let me live long enough to earn more? The teacher says Allah knew it was better for him to die young. Then, says the student, what if the brother who rejected faith cries out, why didn't You take me as a child too? The teacher has no answer. The point the story makes: if you insist human reason can always explain what Allah's justice must do, sooner or later you'll hit a question it can't answer. Historians treat this story with caution, and other reasons for his turn are told too. But the turn itself is the history. Al-Ash'ari left the Mu'tazilah. Some reports say he stood up in the mosque in Basra and announced it in public. What makes him matter is what he did next. He didn't throw away reason. He took the tools of kalam, the careful arguments he'd learned, and turned them toward defending what the people of hadith already held: that the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech, that His attributes are real, that believers will see Him in the life to come. Ahmad ibn Hanbal had answered with a request for a verse. Al-Ash'ari answered with the verse, and an argument to go with it. Reason in the service of tradition. That's the line he drew, and others would follow it.
screen: `A QUESTION REASON CAN'T ANSWER.` · `HE LEAVES THE MU'TAZILAH.` · `HE KEEPS THE TOOLS OF KALAM.` · then, large: `REASON FOR TRADITION.`

segments.voice: The practice: change your mind well. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you once held firmly and see differently now. A view, a habit, a person you misjudged. Notice what changed it: a question, an event, someone who wouldn't let it go. Now look at your old self without contempt. That person was working with what they had. Al-Ash'ari didn't burn his years of study; he kept what was useful and turned it. Is there anything from your old view worth keeping? Stay with that. If you pray, you can thank Allah for whatever led you on. The bell holds the time.
Imam al-Ash'ari. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari: a former Mu'tazili who used reason to defend traditional belief. Today's word.
Your line: reason for tradition. Today, take one thing you've inherited, a habit or a saying, and find one good reason for it. Tomorrow, the Ash'ari school. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sunni students of theology learn about al-Ash'ari as the scholar who left the Mu'tazilah and used kalam to defend the beliefs of the people of hadith, and the Ash'ari school is named after him.
